analogy.p: Think of the four gases as people at a security door who each have a different password. You say a different 'word' (the test) to each, and only the right person replies in the right way: hydrogen replies with a squeaky pop, oxygen with a relit splint, carbon dioxide by turning limewater milky and chlorine by bleaching damp paper. The analogy breaks down because gases are not choosing to respond: the observation is the result of a chemical reaction, and some gases (like nitrogen) simply do not respond to any of the four tests.

bullets: **Hydrogen** (H2): burning splint held at the open end of the test tube; the gas burns with a **squeaky pop**.
**Oxygen** (O2): a **glowing splint** put into the gas **relights**.
**Carbon dioxide** (CO2): bubble the gas through **limewater**; the limewater turns **milky (cloudy)**.
**Chlorine** (Cl2): hold **damp litmus paper** in the gas; it is **bleached white**.
Each answer needs both halves: the test (what you do) AND the observation (what you see). A result on its own earns fewer marks.
Know where each gas comes from, as exam questions give you a reaction and ask which test to use.
The tests are **chemical tests**: they work because of a chemical reaction of the gas, not because of its colour or smell.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.8.2 (Identification of common gases) asks you to **describe the test for four gases: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and chlorine**. Each test must be learned as a pair: the exact thing you do, and the exact result you see. Gas tests are used in analytical chemistry to identify what has been produced in a reaction, which is why they appear in questions about metals with acids, carbonates with acids, electrolysis, decomposition and many unknown-substance puzzles. This is for all students (combined and separate science), so it is a reliable source of easy marks.

bullets: Colourless gases (hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide) cannot be told apart by looking at them, so a **positive test** is required.
A **positive test** gives the expected observation; a **negative test** gives no change, which tells you that gas is not present.
The gases are produced in reactions you already know: metal + acid gives hydrogen; carbonate + acid gives carbon dioxide; electrolysis of brine gives chlorine and hydrogen.
Always **collect the gas first** (in a test tube or gas syringe) before testing, so the test is done on a decent sample.
Tests are done in a set order only if the gas is unknown: splint tests first (they are quick), then limewater, then litmus paper for chlorine in a fume cupboard.
Identification is based on **chemical properties** (how the gas reacts), which is more reliable than physical properties such as smell.
The tests only identify the gases listed. Nitrogen and the noble gases give a negative result with all four tests.
core.h: Why we test for gases and how the tests work
core.p: Many gases are colourless and look identical, so you cannot identify them by eye. A gas test makes the gas do something characteristic: burn, support burning, react to give a solid, or change a coloured indicator. The result is evidence for one particular gas because only that gas gives that observation among the common gases you meet at GCSE. In an exam you must always link the observation to the gas using the exact wording; saying only 'it goes pop' without 'squeaky' or without the burning splint can lose the mark.

bullets: Test: a **lit splint** (it must be burning with a flame), held at the **open end of the test tube**.
Positive result: **squeaky pop**. Do not write just 'pop' or 'explosion'; the word 'squeaky' is in the mark scheme.
Equation: **2H2 + O2 → 2H2O** (hydrogen + oxygen → water). Hydrogen is **oxidised**, oxygen is reduced.
Hydrogen is **less dense than air**, so a test tube of it is held with the **mouth pointing downwards** (inverted) to stop the gas escaping upwards before the splint arrives.
Hydrogen is **flammable**, so only small volumes are used and no naked flames are near the generation apparatus until the test.
Sources of hydrogen: metal + acid (e.g. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2), and the **cathode** (negative electrode) in electrolysis of aqueous solutions of reactive-metal compounds.
Hydrogen is a colourless, odourless gas and the least dense of all gases.
The bigger the sample, the louder the pop, which is why a gas syringe or full test tube is used.
core.p: To test for **hydrogen**, hold a **lit (burning) splint** at the **mouth of the test tube** containing the gas. If the gas is hydrogen it burns rapidly with a **squeaky pop**. The pop happens because hydrogen reacts with the oxygen in the air very quickly: the small amount of hydrogen in the tube burns all at once and the steam produced expands suddenly, making the noise. The equation is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. The product is water, so the inside of the tube may also mist up with water vapour.

bullets: Test: a **glowing splint** (flame blown out, still red hot) placed **into** the test tube.
Positive result: the splint **relights**. Say 'relights', not 'goes out' or 'burns brighter' alone.
Air contains about **21% oxygen** and **78% nitrogen**, which is not enough oxygen to relight a glowing splint.
Oxygen is a colourless, odourless gas that is slightly denser than air.
Oxygen is produced by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide with a **manganese(IV) oxide catalyst**: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2.
Oxygen is also produced at the **anode** (positive electrode) in electrolysis of aqueous solutions (e.g. of sulfates), and by photosynthesis in plants.
Mistake to avoid: a **lit** splint is used for hydrogen; a **glowing** splint is used for oxygen. The two are not interchangeable.
Link: oxygen is needed for combustion, rusting and respiration (see other topics).
core.p: To test for **oxygen**, place a **glowing splint** (a splint that has been lit and the flame blown out so it just glows red) into the test tube of gas. If the gas is oxygen the splint **relights** (bursts back into flame). Oxygen **supports combustion**, and the gas in the tube has a much higher concentration of oxygen than air (air is only about 21% oxygen), so the glowing end burns faster and ignites. The test depends on the oxygen reacting with the hot wood.

bullets: Test: **bubble** the gas through limewater (a delivery tube leads from the reaction vessel into a test tube of limewater).
Positive result: limewater goes **milky / cloudy** (from colourless). Do not write 'goes white' only; milky or cloudy is the key.
Equation: **Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(l)**. The solid calcium carbonate causes the cloudiness.
Limewater is a **dilute solution of calcium hydroxide**; it is colourless before the test.
**Extension (not required by the specification):** if too much CO2 is bubbled in, the milkiness clears again because soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 → Ca(HCO3)2.
Sources of CO2: carbonate + acid (CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2), thermal decomposition of carbonates, combustion of carbon compounds, and respiration.
Carbon dioxide is colourless, odourless and **denser than air**; it puts out a lit splint, but this is **not** the test used for it.
The delivery tube must go **below** the surface of the limewater so the gas actually bubbles through the liquid.
core.p: To test for **carbon dioxide**, bubble the gas through **limewater** (calcium hydroxide solution). If the gas is carbon dioxide the limewater turns **milky (cloudy)**. This happens because carbon dioxide reacts with the dissolved calcium hydroxide to make **calcium carbonate**, which is **insoluble** in water, so it appears as tiny white solid particles suspended in the liquid (a precipitate). The equation is Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O.

bullets: Test: **damp litmus paper** held in (or at the mouth of the container of) the gas.
Positive result: the paper is **bleached white**. If the paper first turns red, say it then goes white; the final colour is what the mark scheme wants.
Reaction with water: **Cl2 + H2O ⇌ HCl + HClO** (extension: the HClO is the bleaching agent).
Chlorine is a **pale green (yellow-green)** gas with a **choking smell**, and it is **toxic**.
The test and any experiment with chlorine must be done in a **fume cupboard** (or very well ventilated space) with only small volumes.
Sources: **electrolysis of sodium chloride solution (brine)** gives chlorine at the anode; also the electrolysis of molten metal chlorides.
Chlorine is a **halogen** (group 7) and is **denser than air**.
It is important to contrast with an acid gas: other acidic gases only turn blue litmus red; chlorine **bleaches** to white.
core.p: To test for **chlorine**, hold a piece of **damp litmus paper** (blue or red) in the gas. Chlorine **bleaches** the paper, turning it **white**. The paper must be damp because chlorine reacts with the water on the paper to form acidic solutions (hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid, HClO). The acid may turn blue litmus red for a moment, but chloric(I) acid then **bleaches** the dye, leaving the paper white. Dry litmus paper is not bleached properly because there is no water for the reaction.

bullets: **Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen**: test with a lit splint (squeaky pop).
**Metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide**: test with limewater.
**Electrolysis of aqueous solutions**: hydrogen at the cathode (if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen), oxygen at the anode (unless a halide is present).
**Electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution)** gives **hydrogen** (cathode), **chlorine** (anode) and sodium hydroxide solution.
**Thermal decomposition of metal carbonates** (e.g. copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide) gives carbon dioxide.
**Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide** with a catalyst gives oxygen.
**Combustion of hydrocarbons** gives carbon dioxide and water.
**Photosynthesis** gives oxygen; **respiration** gives carbon dioxide.
core.h: Where each gas comes from: linking to other topics
core.p: Gas tests are almost always applied to a reaction you can predict. If you know the reactant types you can predict the gas and choose the correct test. This is why questions often give a reaction and ask 'Describe a test to show that the gas formed is...'. Learn these links and you can answer quickly and justify your choice using chemistry.

bullets: Burning splint → **squeaky pop** = **hydrogen**.
Glowing splint → **relights** = **oxygen**.
Limewater → **milky** = **carbon dioxide**.
Damp litmus paper → **bleached** = **chlorine**.
**Two colourless gases that both do nothing to a splint**: nitrogen and carbon dioxide; use limewater to distinguish them (CO2 gives milky).
**A lit splint going out** is observed with CO2 and nitrogen, but is **not** a specific test for either, so never give it as your test.
Only chlorine is coloured (pale green) and has a strong smell, and it is the only one of the four that is a halogen.
If no test gives a positive result, the gas may be nitrogen, a noble gas, or one outside the specification.
core.h: Telling the gases apart: comparing the four tests
core.p: A common exam style is to give you an unknown gas and a list of results, then ask you to identify it. The best approach is to compare tests by what you do (burning or glowing splint, limewater or litmus) and by what happens. Notice that two different splints are used: a **burning (lit) splint** for hydrogen and a **glowing splint** for oxygen. The words are different because the gases do different things: hydrogen burns and oxygen helps other things burn.

bullets: **Gas syringe**: collects a measured volume of any gas; used for rates of reaction experiments.
**Over water** (inverted measuring cylinder or test tube in a trough): works for gases that are **insoluble** in water such as hydrogen and oxygen.
**Downward delivery (upward displacement of air)**: for gases **denser than air**, e.g. carbon dioxide and chlorine; the gas sinks to the bottom of the tube.
**Upward delivery (downward displacement of air)**: for gases **less dense than air**, e.g. hydrogen; the tube is held upside down.
Chlorine is poisonous so is collected in a fume cupboard, usually in a sealed container or gas jar.
Carbon dioxide is moderately soluble in water, so collection over water loses some gas.
Always **remove the delivery tube from the water before stopping the heating** if water is used, to prevent suck-back.
Gas jars with lids are used to collect gas and to carry out the splint test.
core.p: Before testing, the gas must be collected without losing it or contaminating it. The method depends on the gas's **solubility in water** and **density compared with air**. Using the wrong method gives a poor sample. For example, collecting carbon dioxide over water is less effective because some of it dissolves, and collecting chlorine over water is poor because it dissolves and reacts. A gas syringe gives an accurate volume, and is useful when you also have to measure how much gas is made.

bullets: **Hydrogen** is **flammable** and forms explosive mixtures with air: use small volumes, keep flames away from the generator, wear eye protection.
**Chlorine** is **toxic** and can irritate the lungs and eyes: work in a **fume cupboard**, use small amounts, avoid breathing the gas.
**Limewater** is an irritant to eyes (a dilute alkali): wear **eye protection** (goggles).
**Acids** used to make the gases (e.g. dilute hydrochloric acid) are irritants: avoid contact and wear goggles.
A glowing or lit splint is a **burn** and **fire hazard**: dispose of splints in water or on a heatproof mat.
Glass tubes can break or become hot: handle with care and keep apparatus supported in a clamp.
Tie back long hair, keep bags away and keep the workspace tidy.
Never test large volumes of hydrogen; the pop is much louder than students expect.
core.p: Gas tests involve flames, flammable gases, hot splints and, for chlorine, a toxic gas. A good answer on practical safety identifies the specific **hazard**, the **risk** it causes and the **precaution** that controls it. The idea of linking hazard to a precaution is something examiners reward, particularly in longer practical questions.

bullets: Say 'a lit splint gives a **squeaky pop**' rather than 'it explodes' or 'it goes boom'.
Say 'a glowing splint **relights**', not 'it catches fire' (too vague).
Say 'limewater turns **milky / cloudy**' not 'turns white' or 'goes clear'.
Say 'damp litmus paper is **bleached (white)**', not 'turns red' only.
Describe the test using **two parts**: apparatus action + observation.
Name the gas in your conclusion: 'the gas is hydrogen'.
If asked for a chemical explanation, quote the equation and state symbols if requested.
Use correct formulae: H2, O2, CO2, Cl2 (diatomic where relevant).
core.h: Observations and how to describe them with the right words
core.p: Examiners mark the precise vocabulary. The same chemistry described vaguely loses the mark. Practise writing the test and result as one sentence. A reliable template is: 'Hold a (burning/glowing) splint at the mouth of the test tube / bubble the gas through limewater / hold damp litmus paper in the gas. The result is (squeaky pop / relights / limewater turns milky / paper is bleached white).' If asked to justify, add the name of the gas.

bullets: A positive test is **evidence**, not proof, but at GCSE it is accepted as identification.
The tests are **qualitative** (tell you what, not how much); a gas syringe is used for quantity.
A small sample of hydrogen may not pop loudly; repeat or use more gas.
Moisture on the splint or contamination can affect results; use a fresh splint each time.
Use a **control** (e.g. air in a test tube) to show that the splint behaves differently in the unknown gas.
If more than one gas is produced (e.g. electrolysis of brine), you test them separately, usually at separate electrodes.
Link to **purity and formulations**: tests such as these are used to identify products in analysis.
Link to Paper 2 questions on the atmosphere (4.9), which refer to oxygen and carbon dioxide.
core.h: Higher-level reasoning: why the tests are reliable but limited
core.p: A test is only useful if the positive result is unique to one gas. The four tests are reliable for GCSE because the results are distinct, but they have limits. For example, the squeaky-pop test works only if enough hydrogen is present and mixed with air, and the limewater test is positive for CO2 only: sulfur dioxide can also turn limewater cloudy, but that is outside the specification. Always base your decisions on the information given in the question and avoid adding extra gases unless the question suggests them.

exam: 'Describe the test for hydrogen / oxygen / carbon dioxide / chlorine' is typically a **2 mark** question: 1 mark for the test, 1 mark for the positive result.
Learn the four tests as a table with two columns: test and result; revise them until you can write them from memory.
For 'identify the gas' questions in 1-2 marks, give the **name** of the gas and link it to the observation.
For a 3-4 mark question about a practical, use the method: collect the gas, perform the test, state the result, name the gas, and mention a safety precaution.
The command word **describe** means state the method and the observation; **explain** means give the reason, e.g. limewater milky because calcium carbonate (an insoluble precipitate) forms.
Use correct state symbols and balanced equations when asked: Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(l).
If the question gives a diagram, label the apparatus (delivery tube, limewater, boiling tube) and state where the gas bubbles.
In 6-mark questions on analysis, combine gas tests with other tests (flame tests, ion tests, chromatography) and write about each in a clear logical order.
For predict-and-test questions, write the reaction first (metal + acid or carbonate + acid) and then the matching gas test.
For safety questions state the hazard, then the precaution; e.g. chlorine is toxic, so use a fume cupboard.
Data questions may give a table of observations from tests; read it systematically and match each observation to a gas.

mistakes.r: Hydrogen is tested with a burning (lit) splint, giving a squeaky pop.
mistakes.w: Using a glowing splint to test for hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Oxygen is tested with a glowing splint which relights.
mistakes.w: Using a lit splint to test for oxygen or saying the splint 'goes out'.

mistakes.r: Limewater turns milky / cloudy when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
The test for carbon dioxide is limewater turning milky; a splint going out is not specific.
mistakes.w: Saying 'a lit splint going out' is the test for carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Damp litmus paper is bleached white by chlorine.
mistakes.w: Using dry litmus paper for chlorine, or saying it turns red.

mistakes.r: State what you do AND what you see.
mistakes.w: Giving the observation without the test (or the test without the observation).

mistakes.r: A squeaky pop is the standard answer.
The gas must be bubbled through the limewater.
mistakes.w: Holding the limewater and the gas separately (not bubbling).

mistakes.r: Chlorine is a diatomic molecule, Cl2.
mistakes.w: Writing the formula of chlorine as Cl.

summary: You must be able to describe the test and positive result for four gases: hydrogen (lit splint, squeaky pop), oxygen (glowing splint relights), carbon dioxide (limewater turns milky) and chlorine (damp litmus paper bleached white). These tests identify gases made in common reactions and are reliable marks in Paper 2.

terms.d: A test that gives the expected observation, showing the substance is present.
A test that gives no change, so the substance is not present.
A wooden splint with a flame; used in the test for hydrogen.
A splint that was lit and then blown out so it glows red; used in the test for oxygen.
The sound made when hydrogen burns rapidly with oxygen in air; the positive test for hydrogen.
A dilute solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2; used to test for carbon dioxide.
An insoluble solid formed in a solution by a chemical reaction; calcium carbonate makes limewater milky.
Paper containing an acid–base indicator; blue in alkali, red in acid; bleached by chlorine.
To remove the colour from a substance; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.
A reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and releases energy; oxygen supports it.
An enclosed, ventilated workspace that removes harmful gases such as chlorine.
Poisonous; harmful to health if breathed in, swallowed or absorbed.
Easily set on fire; hydrogen is flammable.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up; manganese(IV) oxide in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
Made of molecules containing two atoms, e.g. H2, O2, Cl2.
Apparatus used to collect and measure a volume of gas.

worked.ans: Hold a lit splint at the open end of a test tube of the gas; a squeaky pop shows the gas is hydrogen.
worked.q: Describe how you would test a gas to show it is hydrogen. (2 marks)
steps: Test: use a burning (lit) splint held at the mouth of the test tube of gas.
Result: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.

worked.ans: Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky. CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2
worked.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and a gas is given off. Describe how to show the gas is carbon dioxide and write a balanced equation for the reaction. (4 marks)
steps: Use a delivery tube to bubble the gas through limewater (1).
Reaction: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide (1).
Balanced equation: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 (1).

worked.ans: First gas: oxygen. The limewater did not turn milky so the second gas is not carbon dioxide. Chlorine is toxic, so use a fume cupboard.
worked.q: A student collects a colourless gas. A glowing splint is placed in the gas and relights. The student then bubbles another colourless gas from the same experiment through limewater and sees no change. Identify the first gas and state what the second result shows. Give a precaution when testing chlorine. (4 marks)
steps: Splint relights → the first gas is oxygen (1).
Limewater unchanged → carbon dioxide is not present in the second gas (1).
Chlorine is toxic (1) so the test is carried out in a fume cupboard (1).
